title: datasette-arrows 0.1a0
content:
Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0

Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats.

I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it.

Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot.

Add the plugin to Datasette (datasette install datasette-arrows) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option:

This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release.

title: ★ The 50-Yard Line
content:
Ever since the Huang/Nvidia scandal erupted, I’ve been thinking about a short post I wrote back in March, under the headline “Jensen Huang Doesn’t Smell Anything”:

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, during an on-stage interview at The Hill & Valley Forum last summer, was asked “What do you see as America’s unique advantages that other countries don’t have?”

His answer, after taking a moment to think, “America’s unique advantage that no country could possibly have is President Trump.”

Huang, newly appointed to the aforelinked President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, seemingly doesn’t smell the growing stink.

The stink was the historically low (and sinking) popularity to which Trump’s 2.0 presidency had sunk. Undeniable to anyone in touch with reality. Huang’s obsequious Trump-fellating answer to that question would have been eye-catching even when Trump first rolled back into office with an aggressive agenda and a surplus of political capital from a clear election victory — but it was, frankly, a startling thing to say at any point. It makes a lot more sense, though, given what’s come to light in the last 10 days.

If you’re not paying close attention you might think Huang’s was the sort of answer any major tech CEO might have given. But it’s not. That was a really unusual thing for Huang to say, way out of line with how corporate leaders typically approach politics. The typical approach for large publicly held corporations is to avoid partisan politics. Advocate only for policies directly related to the company’s business, and otherwise stay out. The political winds change direction every few years. George Bush senior in 1988 was the last new president elected from the same party as the outgoing incumbent, and he only lasted one term. It makes no sense for a corporation that intends to continue thriving for more than the next few years to closely align itself with one party — unless they believe that party will remain in power for the foreseeable future, à la the FDR/Truman Democrats, who won five consecutive presidential elections from 1932 to 1948 (and seven out of nine through 1968).

One metaphor I use for politics is a football field. Democrats on the left, Republicans on the right. CEOs typically stay as close as they can to the 50-yard line in the middle of the field. That way, when an election puts the other party in power, they don’t have to move — they just need to turn around. That’s how someone like Tim Cook could maintain good relations with the White House from Obama to Trump to Biden back to Trump again. He just stayed close to midfield and turned around after each election.

Remaining as close as possible to political midfield under Trump required unseemly obsequious tribute, unprecedented in modern U.S. history. Million-dollar tickets to his inauguration. That ridiculous gold trophy. Embarrassing stuff. But that’s ultimately a reflection of Trump’s avarice, not the politics of Cook personally or Apple as a company. That was the price to stay on the 50-yard line. Cook has often repeated that his two personal heroes are Martin Luther King Jr. and Bobby Kennedy (senior, to be clear). He keeps portraits of both of them in his office. He never swapped them out for portraits of, say, Ronald Reagan. Apple never changed its internal policies or language regarding racial and LGBT equality. The Apple homepage never stopped celebrating Martin Luther King Jr. Day — even when it coincided with Trump’s second inauguration.

And yet Trump remains so enamored of Cook that he floated his name to succeed Huang at Nvidia. Tim Apple remains the apple of Trump’s eye. Yet Apple had nothing to change or apologize for when Biden came into office, nor will they again if, as now seems likely, Trump is succeeded in 2029 by a Democrat elected to clean up his kakistocratic kleptomaniacal mess. (Presumably Apple will gladly pony up at least another $25 million to restore the East Wing after Trump’s architecturally ungodly ballroom edifice is torn down.) And Apple certainly won’t need lawyers to defend them from charges of corruption and/or breaches of national security. Nvidia, not so much.

This is what we should want: business leaders who endeavor to stay out of partisan politics, not hopelessly enmesh themselves in it. Industry and politics cannot operate in isolation, but they should avoid intertwinement except where necessary. Great companies stand the test of time. That’s not feasible if you hitch your corporate wagon to one party or the other, no matter the political moment. We don’t think of Procter & Gamble, Coca-Cola, or Berkshire Hathaway as being Democratic or Republican companies. You cannot chart their fortunes over time based on which party was in power in any given decade. You may well have strong political opinions that are far from the 50-yard line, on one side or the other. I do. But you shouldn’t look for those opinions to be validated by industry executives, any more than you should look for business and product-design decisions to be made by elected government officials. True American values put country over party when it comes to business. And, as Calvin Coolidge aptly put it, “The chief business of the American people is business.”

America does possess unique advantages that other countries don’t have. Personal liberties enshrined in our Bill of Rights. A vibrant, diverse, ever-changing melting pot of a citizenry. A strong tradition of the rule of law, placing no man above it. Competitive markets that allow new entrants to supplant entrenched incumbents. Any CEO worth their salt should have an answer to the question of America’s unique advantages that holds true no matter who, from which party, is currently president. And they should believe it.

What makes Huang’s answer so off-putting isn’t that it was so abjectly partisan — politically tone-deaf to the inevitability of Democrats coming back into power, and perversely obsequious to Trump personally — but that Donald Trump is the antithesis to the entire above list of things that actually give America unique advantages other countries don’t have. Trump and the MAGA movement are also decidedly American and uniquely so, but they represent what’s worst about America.

But I give Huang credit for honesty. Clearly, he believed what he said. Huang didn’t just stray from the 50-yard line — he broke for Trump’s end zone.
description: CEOs typically stay as close as they can to the 50-yard line in the middle of the political playing field. That way, when an election puts the other party in power, they don’t have to move — they just need to turn around.

title: If the Windows documentation doesn’t list a particular technology as supporting an operation, does that mean that it doesn’t support it?
content:
In the Windows documentation for various file system operations, you will often find a section in the Remarks that says

This function is supported by the following technologies.

Technology Supported
Server Message Block (SMB) 3.0 protocol Yes
SMB 3.0 Transparent Failover (TFO) Yes
SMB 3.0 with Scale-out File Shares (SO) Yes
Cluster Shared Volume File System (CsvFS) Yes
Resilient File System (ReFS) Yes

But what about network protocols that aren’t on the list? Does their absence mean that they aren’t supported?

The table lists the file systems and network protocols that we has information for. If something is not on the list, that doesn’t mean that it doesn’t support it. It just means that we don’t know whether it supports it.

If it definitely didn’t support it, then it would have been in the table with a “No”, like this one for Get­File­Information­By­Handle:

Technology Supported
Server Message Block (SMB) 3.0 protocol No
SMB 3.0 Transparent Failover (TFO) No
SMB 3.0 with Scale-out File Shares (SO) No
Cluster Shared Volume File System (CsvFS) Yes
Resilient File System (ReFS) Yes

Since third parties can implement their own network protocols,¹ the Windows documentation cannot be comprehensive. It just documents what it knows. If you want information about some other network protocol or file system driver, you’ll have to consult the documentation for the product that implements the protocol or file system you are interested in.

¹ I noticed AFS and APFS and I didn’t even make it to the letter B.

The post If the Windows documentation doesn’t list a particular technology as supporting an operation, does that mean that it doesn’t support it? appeared first on The Old New Thing.

title: Supersequences and Superpermutations
content:
A word is universal if it contains every permutation of its alphabet as a subsequence: the letters must appear in order, but gaps are allowed.

For example, you can find all six permutations of the digits 1, 2, and 3 inside the string 1231213. Not all permutations can be found as a contiguous substring—that would be a superpermutation—but all can be found as a subsequence.

The word

01234567890123456780293451670823451960782134506978231405678213904567823109456782301

is universal for the set of 10 digits. This word was discovered some time ago, but Jason Davies has recently proved that this the smallest universal word on 10 digits. It has 83 characters, and Davies proved that no word of 82 characters is universal over the digits. See his paper here.

I’m surprised that all 10! = 3,628,800 permutations of 10 digits can be found as subsequences of such a relatively short word.

Universal words, or supersequences, are easily confused with superpermutations. See OEIS sequences A062714 and A180632. Minimal length superpermuations are necessarily longer than minimal length supersequences [1] since the requirements on the former are stricter, requiring permutations to appear as contiguous substrings and not merely as subsequences. In other words, every superpermutation is a supersequence, but not vice versa.

For example,

123412314231243121342132413214321

is a minimal superpermutation on four symbols while

123412314213

is a minimal supersequence.

Note that it’s trivial to produce a supersequence: just concatenate all n! permutations of the symbols into one sequence. But finding minimal supersequences and minimal superpermutations is challenging.

 

[1] For n = 1 or 2 the minimal supersequence and minimal superpermutation are the same. For n > 2 they are not.

title: Email Dumpster Diving
content:
Sometimes, for fun, I like to go rummage around in my email’s Spam folder.

Why? Who knows (probably a question for a licensed medical professional).

I think there’s some part of me that chases the dopamine hit of finding a “needle in the haystack”: an email flagged as spam that shouldn’t be (which almost never happens, so I guess this behavior falls under the label of addictive/impulsive seeking).

I think there’s also a part of me that enjoys keeping a finger on the pulse of scam tactics, like “Let’s see how people are trying to trick me today…” Almost like a form of inoculation: deliberate exposure to scam tactics in a controlled environment. It helps me develop an immunity, which comes in handy when family members come to me with their emails and ask, “Is this legit?”

Here’s a little exposure to what I’ve seen recently.

First: I see a lot of emails that exploit the way cloud services bill us. For example: “You’ve hit your limits! Better log in or you’ll lose access!” Or, “Your credit card has expired. Better log in and enter your new credit card so you can keep doing what you’re doing.” ⁣

(Note the little green banner at the top — “This message was sent from a trusted sender.” A kind of “Why would I deceive you?”)

These emails are interesting not only as an exercise in analyzing scam tactics, but also as a meta-commentary on legitimate software use cases.

For example, isn’t it interesting how difficult it can be to distinguish scammer tactics from legitimate software company practices? “Hey, you better give us your credit card or you’ll lose access to your thing!” That’s what ransomware is; it’s also what SaaS is, lol.

It’s kinda funny, yeah? No, just me? Ok, I digress. Next email.

This is an interesting one. Usually phishing emails are pretty overt in their intentions: click this big button and get taken to a page where you do what we want, e.g. enter sensitive info like a password or credit card. (Again, interesting that legitimate marketing teams follow the same strategy lol. It’s called a “CTA”: click here and do what we want.)

In this case, however, the email claims to be from a “Gina Rinehart” and tries to establish credibility by saying, “Look I’m a real person! Here’s a link to my Wikipedia page.” No CTA to a sus web page here at all.

I do wonder what would happen if I emailed back. I’m sure somewhere down that road is a solicitation for my bank info or the like. I’d love to mess with them, but I got better things to do with my time (like write this blog post).

Ok, last email. I came across this one in my Spam folder:

“Oh interesting,” I thought. “Somebody is trying to ride the Trump Accounts initiative from the current administration and trick folks into divulging sensitive information.” Makes sense. Totally plausible vector for attack.

But then as I do my email forensics (examine where the links point to, inspect the sender, etc.) I find something surprising:

Turns out, service.govdelivery.com is a legitimate domain and irs@ service.govdelivery.com is listed on the IRS’ website as the official sender for their bulletins. (The email headers check out too.)

On top of that, the CTAs in the email all point to officially sanctioned websites, App Store apps, etc. In other words: this is actually a legitimate email from the United States Government that was flagged as Spam in Gmail, lol.

And there it is: my needle in the haystack. The dopamine hit I need to continue with this ridiculous, fun, and informative habit.
